results.title: Augmentation of EEG and ECG Time Series for Deep Learning Applications: Integrating Changepoint Detection into the iAAFT Surrogates - ADS
results.content: ## Augmentation of EEG and ECG Time Series for Deep Learning Applications: Integrating Changepoint Detection into the iAAFT Surrogates. This is especially the case for physiological time series, which are both noisy and scarce, which calls for data augmentation to artificially increase the size of datasets. This is achieved by combining offline changepoint detection with the iterative amplitude-adjusted Fourier transform (iAAFT), which ensures that the time-frequency properties of the original signal are preserved during augmentation. The proposed method is validated through comparisons of the performance of i) a deep learning seizure detection algorithm on both the original and augmented versions of the CHB-MIT and Siena scalp electroencephalography (EEG) databases, and ii) a deep learning atrial fibrillation (AF) detection algorithm on the original and augmented versions of the Computing in Cardiology Challenge 2017 dataset. By virtue of the proposed method, for the CHB-MIT and Siena datasets respectively, accuracy rose by 4.4% and 1.9%, precision by 10% and 5.5%, recall by 3.6% and 0.9%, and F1 by 4.2% and 1.4%.

Title: Mastering Nonstationary Time Series Analysis: Methods and Techniques
Mastering Nonstationary Time Series Analysis: Methods and Techniques. # Mastering Nonstationary Time Series Analysis: Methods and Techniques. By understanding and correctly identifying the nonstationary elements in a time series, analysts can apply suitable methods, such as differencing, transformation, or advanced modeling techniques like ARIMA and GARCH, to mitigate these challenges. ## Understanding Trends in Time Series Data. Identifying and understanding these trends is crucial for analyzing nonstationary time series data, as they can significantly influence the forecasting and modeling processes. To identify trends in time series data, several methods can be employed. Decomposition techniques, such as seasonal decomposition of time series (STL), break down the data into trend, seasonal, and residual components, allowing for a more structured analysis. Incorporating these methods into time series analysis enhances the ability to accurately model and forecast nonstationary data, recognizing and accounting for the underlying trends that drive the observed patterns. Understanding and accounting for seasonality is crucial for accurate analysis and forecasting in nonstationary time series. These predictable changes can significantly impact the overall trend and variability of a time series, making it essential to identify and model them effectively. Incorporating methods for detecting and handling structural breaks ensures a more robust and accurate analysis of nonstationary time series, ultimately leading to more reliable insights and decisions based on the data. Unit root tests are fundamental tools in the analysis of time series data, specifically designed to detect the presence of nonstationarity. In summary, unit root tests like the ADF, PP, and KPSS are essential for determining the nonstationarity of time series data. Understanding and applying these tests correctly is crucial for accurate time series analysis, helping researchers and analysts build more reliable models. In the realm of nonstationary time series analysis, detrending techniques are crucial for transforming data into a stationary format, which is essential for accurate modeling and forecasting. **Logarithmic Transformation** is another popular method, especially useful for time series data exhibiting exponential growth or multiplicative seasonality. Analyzing these data sets using techniques like structural break tests and seasonal decomposition allows researchers to identify underlying patterns and abrupt changes, thus facilitating more accurate climate modeling and prediction.

Further, to this end, we test the hypothesis that signatures of nonstationarity in rainfall extremes do not ne-cessitate the use of nonstationary IDFs for design considera-tions. Spatial distribution of trends, change points, and nonstationarities in rainfall extremes of several durations in nine urbanized locations, Southern Ontario (a–g). There are several reasons for selecting warm periods: ﬁrst, extreme rainfall events mostly occur in the study area during the warm season (Cheng et al., 2010); second, the focus of our analysis is an investigation of extreme rainfall related ﬂood risks and development of IDF curves using extreme rainfall statistics. While for Toronto International Air-port and Hamilton Airport, we ﬁnd no increase in the short-duration rainfall extremes of less than 1 h and the 50-year return period considering the nonstationary condition, the in-crease is more pronounced for longer durations and return periods (12 and 24 h, and the 50- and 100-year return peri-ods; Sect. On the other hand, except for the 100-year re-turn period events, the hourly precipitation extremes in Lon-don International Airport, in general, show a decrease in the ratio (Tables S23.1–23.2) across all return periods, which is predominantly due to the presence of signiﬁcant downward trends with change points in the time series. Preliminary investigations based on regional and global climate model simulations in the study area conﬁrm a con-siderable uncertainty in the projection of short-duration and high-intensity extreme rain events (Coulibaly et al., 2015). The statistical uncertainty in modelling nonstationarity can result from multiple sources, for instance, extrapolat-ing the effects detected with observed historical series to the more extreme values that have not yet been experienced, model choices resulting from selection of covariates in the nonstationary distributions (Agilan and Umamahesh, 2017), and the treatment of nonstationarity introduced through ei-ther a linear (Ali and Mishra, 2017; Cheng et al., 2014; Wes-tra et al., 2012) or polynomial (Villarini et al., 2009b) trend, or a change point (Renard et al., 2013) in the model.
